Mr. Speaker, after this bit of by-play my contribution to this debate may appear to be a sort of anticlimax. Sitting in this corner as I do, surrounded by hon. gentlemen of socialist mentality, I must say that I sometimes feel like Daniel in the lions' den. I do believe the question just put to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) was rather well taken. I agree with the hon. member that any over-all social service scheme perhaps would have to be on a federal basis; but the question asked was why a provincial government, which is also able to tax the people for revenue, should impose the means test for an extra $2.50 a month. That was the question, and it cannot be answered by saying it must be done on a national basis.
The answer is that the province of Saskatchewan is short of revenue; we may as well admit that. So are other provinces that cannot augment the present old age pension. There is no mystery about that. Saskatchewan is not as fortunate as some other provinces, which are able to collect higher revenues. British Columbia, I understand, has a sales tax. Saskatchewan had one and then took it off.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE TO STUDY
speechtext: Does the hon. member not know that Saskatchewan's revenues today are $55 million, the highest in its history, and that it still has the sales tax, which yesterday was increased by one cent?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE TO STUDY
speechtext:
If that is so it is all right with me. I am not quarrelling with Saskatchewan; let them run their own business. All I am saying is that to use the argument that it must be done on a national basis is but to avoid the question of whether the means test must be imposed by Saskatchewan if the pension is to be increased by $2.50; so I say that answer is not well taken. However, I will let those hon. gentlemen fight it out between themselves.
Some of us have been sitting in this house for a long time, Mr. Speaker, and some of us

on the opposition side have been waiting patiently for many years to have the government in office bring down some legislation that would eclipse in proportion what I have termed over the years as the miserly old age pension scheme we have today. Each election the Liberals go to the country saying, "Put us in and we will do something to better the lot of the aged." I have kept a record of the advertising that has been carried on for several past elections, dating back to 1935; and almost every election the same thing occurs.
Now, I am saying this for a purpose. The other day the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) asked a question of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) concerning what might be done for the incurables. What was the answer? The minister's answer was that this subject is continually under review by the government. Of course, that is no answer. What is responsible government supposed to do but review things, and on the basis of their review bring down legislation? If the review had only occupied about six months, the answer might have some merit. Since the review must have been going on for the last ten years or more, I do not believe that sort of answer is good enough. Surely, if the government has been reviewing the question of old age pensions, even under a contributory scheme, they should be in a position today to bring down definite legislation covering their proposals and policies.
It is for this reason that some of us believe this motion to set up a committee becomes a sort of red herring drawn across the trail to attract attention, to make people believe we are about to do something, the only result being to delay the start of a better old age pension scheme. I am in agreement with some of those who have spoken today in saying that, if the government has been reviewing this question over a period of ten or fifteen years, they surely have the facts and figures before them. They must have these facts and figures in sufficient detail that, even though the committee is set up, they could not get them in any greater detail. If that is not so, then the government has failed in its attempt to adequately review the situation.
I am going to suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the reason for having this committee investigate the matter of old age pensions according to the terms of reference is that the government has reached the limit of its ability to tax the people of Canada. They say, "We know that if we are to bring in a better old age pension scheme, it is going to cost a tremendous amount of money." The next question is, where is the money to come from?
Old Age Security	*
The people cannot be taxed any more, and that is the government's problem. They say, "We shall go further and bring in a contributory scheme of old age pensions; by that means we will shift the burden from the general tax revenues, and place it upon the people who pay into a designated fund called the old age pension fund." What they are really saying is that they will not tax the whole nation in the sense it is being done today; they will not raise the taxes of the nation as would have to be done in order to bring in a better scheme. But the people will be taxed in another way. By adopting a contributory scheme, the people would have to pay into that fund, which of course is just another form of taxation. Then the government would argue that the more the people can put into this fund, the more they will be able to draw out. I suppose that might be logical.
I am not so confident as the minister seems to be that this will lead to progressive legislation. I believe it could be regarded as a way of escaping responsibility, because the government cannot put in a more elaborate scheme without raising taxation. This, therefore, is just a way of escape for responsible government, by bringing in a contributory scheme and shifting the burden of taxation from the ordinary revenue to the old age pension fund.
I do not know whether this question has occurred to the government, but I should like to ask what they consider the purpose of an economic system is. It seems to me that the purpose of an economic system is to give the highest standard of living and security that the production of the nation is able to obtain for the people; in other words, the goods and services the nation is able to produce and distribute. How does this government operate the economic system, or any other government that might replace it which would have the same monetary mentality? Under our present administration, the way it works is simply this: We reach a high capacity of production, and then when our people do not have the money to buy it we attempt to get rid of it in a series of ways, instead of devising a distributive system that would make it available. Surpluses continue to pile up, and unemployment becomes prevalent. We then have low incomes and unemployment in the midst of abundance. The government begins to sweat and stew about what it is going to do.
Then, of course, they look at our aged citizens with heads bowed in shame and say, "We are sorry; although there are plenty of the necessities of life, we cannot give you more than a pittance." That is the picture,

Old Age Security
and I do not think anyone will gainsay that picture. What is going to happen under the proposed contributory scheme if the financial policy is not changed? The old-line party thinkers will look at our aged people and say, "It is your own fault; here you are in the midst of abundance with no pension to draw upon. You did not contribute enough in the past." I believe that is what will be said. Not only is the government shifting the burden of taxation, but they intend to shift the responsibility.
Let me say this, that personally I do not think it takes any brains to run a government under a taxation system. Surely it does not take any brains to say, "We will do just what we are able to pay for and that will be counted in terms of how much we are able to get out of the taxpayer." It does not take any brains to work that out. Any schoolboy could figure that one. He goes downtown to buy some marbles or something and he says, "I can buy only the marbles for which I have money to pay." That is schoolboy stuff. It does not take any brains for a government to run a nation's business if they have the ability through legislation to stick a gun in the taxpayer's ribs and say, "Now, pay up; we need so much money to run the country." It does not take brains; it takes a little gall and political acumen to do it and still stay in office.
What is going to happen under a contributory scheme to those who cannot contribute? What is going to happen to those who have been transients in bygone years through no fault of their own? What is going to happen to those farmers who are on submarginal lands? Some of us know of these farmers who in days gone by lived on a starvation level. I am not one to paint harsh and dark pictures when there is no need, but we remember how in the thirties the farmers were coming to us. They were mortgaged to the hilt, prices were depressed, crops were not good and the mortgage companies were going to take their land. They came to us almost on bended knees and said, "Isn't there something you can do?" That was the reason the Aberhart administration brought in a moratorium on debt-simply to save the farmers.
It was not until war broke out and prices began to rise that the farmers were able to get out of debt and retain their farms. How are they going to contribute to a contributory scheme when there are no crops or prices are depressed?

Does that bring them money? In the United States they dye their potatoes blue. Does that bring them money? These are the questions I am asking these hon. gentlemen who say the only source of money is production. Let them answer

that. If they cannot answer that, then they will never broaden the old age pension scheme and bring the security and contentment to our people that this wealthy productive country is able to give them.
Once again I am saying the only group in this house that can answer that question is the Social Credit group. There you have it. You have to tax or you have to get the money in some other way, shift the burden, contributory pensions. You have got to do it in that way or listen to us. It is either one thing or the other. Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to see this resolution on the order paper. Before your comments, sir, I had thought that the subamendment offered by the hon. member for Maeleod was one that had a good deal of merit, and which certainly would have received my support. 1 did gather from the amendment that there were by-elections in the offing, and that the hon. member had probably guessed that this was a good time for it.
The amendment would seem to indicate that, because from reading the resolution I

gathered that it provided ample opportunity to discuss almost anything within its scope. In any event I am happy to see that now for the first time in twenty-five years we have an opportunity to deal with what I consider to be our foremost domestic problem, and one that has very great implications.
Here is an opportunity for a committee to make a comprehensive examination into the pension schemes in Canada today. Anyone who knows what we have by way of pensions in this country will surely agree with me when I say that our plans at the present time are not only unbalanced but overlap and, in some ways, compete. We have the federal and provincial old age plan, with the means test; we have the employer-initiated plans in this country; we have the union-negotiated plans. Along with that we have to some extent provincial supplements.
This resolution in my opinion gives us an opportunity to take stock, to see what we have done up until now, and to recommend what we ought to do in the future. As the minister pointed out, for twenty-three years we have been building a welfare state- and I emphasize the word "welfare". I conceive it to be the duty of a modern state to ensure the security and welfare of its citizens; and the desire for economic security in old age, in one form or another, is generally looked upon as one of the normal desires of enlightened human beings.
I am a believer in social security and I am a believer in the welfare state. I would remind hon. members, particularly those sitting on this side of the house, that we were the welfare-state party at the last election, and that the people endorsed us overwhelmingly. So I take this opportunity to do what I have wanted to do before, namely, to protest emphatically against statements made in this chamber or in the other place that by extending welfare by way of further social security we are making of Canadians a nation of leaners, that we are pampering them and coddling them, that we are making them soft and taking away from them their initiative.
I have heard that story twice in my generation. I remember hearing it in the thirties, when it was my responsibility from 1929 to 1939 to look after the welfare of people in Ontario, through the operations of various offices I held, particularly my provincial office. At that time it was my direct duty to look after their welfare-to feed them and to clothe them. I remember well that when we decided to increase the relief we were told we were making people soft. When we decided to make the allowances in cash rather than by chit we were told that

the recipients would spend the money and use it for things other than food.
I remember these stories; but I also remember that there was a war in 1939, and that our enemies never looked upon Canadians as soft. No one ever suggested that we did not have the proper initiative to become the arsenal of democracy. And so when I hear this talk once again in my own generation I know exactly how it should be treated- because I do not believe that social security makes bums out of people. I do not believe that unemployment insurance makes bums out of the unemployed.
Is there anyone in Canada who believes that we were better off before we had old age pensions, unemployment insurance or family allowances? Does anyone suggest that the social legislation of the last three administrations has been bad for Canada, or that we have not been able to afford it, or that it is beyond our means?
I said it was a natural desire for everyone to want a measure of security. Our own personal security is threatened when we are in want, when we suffer from ill health or when we reach old age and are unable to work. That condition breeds instability, anxiety and fear-and fear is a very contagious thing.
I conceive that this resolution gives the committee an opportunity to make recommendations in keeping with the times, so that we may arrive at a new era of long-term security for the individual, and so that no one need have any fear of spending his declining years in poverty or disability.
There are in our society two groups who need our help most at the present time; they are the young, and they are the old. We must provide for each of them according to their needs, and compatibly with our ability. But we must not prefer one to the other.
Let me remind the house that there is no reversal in the security trend in the world. If there is any lesson we can learn from the British election, it is that all the parties and the people endorsed the social security measures which, by the way, are one generation in advance of ours. Remember that.
I agree with the minister that we must wait for the dominion-provincial conference. There are problems which must be solved-financial problems and constitutional problems. But we can be heartened by the last meeting which was held early in January, and which indicated to all of us that there were around the council table men of good will who meant to come to an agreement, and who know that they must come to an agreement. Because we now have upon us not only the old and the near old, but we have the industrial workers,
Old Age Security
we have management, and we have finance, all of whom are more united than they have ever been in their lives. They are converging upon us wanting leadership and action with respect to pensions, because the shoe is beginning to pinch a little for the industrialist and the financier.
The committee has a job of great magnitude and of tremendous scope to perform. It need not be concerned with constitutional and economic problems. But the matter of pensions is one of the great human problems with which we have to deal. It is true that we require a knowledge of the plans of other countries-a knowledge of all plans, both private and public. I agree with the speakers who have said that the committee must produce a national over-all retirement plan. I believe that plan must compare in scope, purpose and effect with the Archambault report which was a landmark for thoroughness in its own field.
Most of the objections that have been raised today by the opposition have carried the suggestion that we are stalling, that we are playing for time. I say to the house that if that were true I would be the first to protest. This is too important a matter for us to be stalling on it. I believe it was the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) who said that we have plenty of information available. How much do we know about pension plans in Canada? I should like to refer to the dominion bureau of statistics, an organization which ought to know. In their reference papers issued in December, 1949, they say:
There is little information available on the cost and the adequacy of protection provided by employees' pension plans in Canadian industries.
Evidently the dominion bureau of statistics does not know all the answers as to the various pension plans in the Dominion of Canada. I conceive that the committee will make recommendations to provide adequately for the old by way of a retirement pension which will at the same time be a basis for industrial pensions. Any recommendation will have to be tailored to our future needs in an expanding economy, and it must cover every person in the country no matter where he finds himself.
How many pension plans are there in Canada? I think the house will be interested to know that at the present time there are 464. Of those 64 per cent, or 293, were established during the war. I call that to your attention particularly because it is an important aspect. Sixty-four per cent of our present operative plans came into effect during the war. Perhaps you know the reason. During the war years wages could not be raised but pensions could be granted. Employers wanted to hold their employees. Possibly other people were

Old Age Security
offering them more money, so employers provided for pensions. There was also such a thing as excess profits taxes and they were minimized by the provision of pensions. All the money they were paying out for pensions in the war years was deductible as it is now, except that at that time there was more of it. Therefore these pension plans grew. We have a responsibility with respect to them which I will point out later on.
Of these plans 455 were contributory and nine were non-contributory, and as to the 455 contributory plans all took advantage of the tax exemption which they were entitled to under the income tax law. I assure hon. members that the more thought you give to the pension problem the more complex and difficult it becomes. I confess that I do not know all the answers. I am not as fortunate as the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) who seems to have many answers to the problem.

speechtext: You have got a lot to learn from him yet.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE TO STUDY
speechtext:
There is one thing I do know. I know that the many-headed monster called the means test certainly must go as a result of any committee that we set up at this session of the house. I think it is far too late for anyone to attempt to bolster the means test by raising the question of permissive earnings or by saying that it is generous in many respects. It is more generous than some other plans, but it is just a question of which of two teeth that are hurting hurts more. Neither should be there.
I say to the minister that the means test has been discredited; its time has run out; but in any event people will not have any part of it any more. They have made up their minds on that point. I was very glad to see that the legislature of Manitoba passed a resolution on Tuesday of this week endorsing a contributory system and at the same time suggesting that the means test should be done away with. In the past our greatest opposition to doing away with the means test has come from industrialists and financiers, but there is a remarkable and rather interesting change. In the Globe and Mail of March 3 there is a report of a pension dispute in Windsor between the Ford Motor Company and the United Automobile Workers. They could not agree on the amount and the newspaper article says that they came down here to see the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) in order to discuss the means test with him. There is one part of the article which is significant, and which reads:
The delegation came here at the suggestion of the company, and were accompanied by Wallace Clark, personnel director of Ford Motor Company.

They are the people who want the means test removed, and they are just as emphatic about it as their workers. As a matter of fact, I have considerable information here that is rather enlightening. For instance, there is a report on the Bank of Nova Scotia monthly review in the Toronto Telegram of March 3, and in it are these words:
It Is widely felt that contributory schemes encourage self-respect, that the absence of a "means test" allows other forms of saving and removes the stigma of pauperism . . .
While I am on that subject I might as well let you have it all. May I refer now to an article in the Ottawa Journal of January 27 which reads in part:
"A minimum needs" pension without a means test was suggested today by H. D. Burns, president of the Crown Life Insurance Company . . .
My object in reading these to you at this time is to indicate that those who are opposed to doing away with the means test are thinning out. The numbers in their ranks are becoming less and less, and now we find ourselves in the position where industrialists and financiers are advocating the taking away of the means test. Mind you, they may have a motive. I do not suggest that they have not a motive, but I am not concerned with their motives. I agree with them. Certainly it is going to be cheaper for them if we do away with the means test, but at the same time if we are serving the public what right have we to look for a motive? When you look around today it is difficult to find anyone who is in favour of the means test. The only answer you get is that we cannot afford it, that it is beyond our capacity. I was not here when old age pensions were first introduced, but I have read the record, and they said the same thing then. I certainly know they said it about family allowances, they have repeated it, and some of them are still repeating it despite the fact that family allowances are here, we require them, and we can afford them.
The usual thing that one hears is that we must have a contributory system. We say "contributory" quickly and glibly and it sounds very good; everybody seems to agree with you about it. But there is nothing magical about a contributory system. In the first place you have to consider how much a man can contribute. We say that a man should not spend more than 25 per cent of what he earns for housing and yet there are very few who can secure housing at that figure. We say that a man should not spend on food more than 25 per cent of what he earns, and yet there are very few who can purchase the food they need for that amount. We must not forget that we have to leave something in a man's envelope for him to take home. The word "contributory" means

so many things to so many of us. If we mean the insurance principle, then all he receives is what he pays for, and I assure you it will take him all of thirty years in order to buy himself a pension of $40 a month. If, on the other hand, we mean the public treasury, to which everyone contributes, then that is another matter entirely. In the common comparison that is made at the present time people say, "Well, let us have contributory retirement pensions in the same way that we have unemployment insurance." That is a great fallacy; people just do not understand the exact problem when they say that. That is one reason I think it important that we should take our time and discuss this problem so that people may learn and understand it.
It must not be forgotten that unemployment insurance was introduced about ten years ago. For the first nine months no money at all was paid out; it was just collected. Then for nine years it was all "put" and very little "take", with the result that the fund was built up to the extent of $600 million; and it was not until February of this year that expenses were even a little higher than receipts.
The problem is very different with respect to retirement pensions. Pensions have to start payment immediately. The old are here; the others are becoming older at the same time, and there is no ten-year period in which to build up a fund. We have to start paying immediately. The usual retiring age in this country is considered to be sixty-five, but the life expectancy of men is twelve years greater than that and of women fourteen years greater. Surely the increased longevity is something that should give us comfort and pleasure. It cannot possibly be a matter of either regret or neglect on our part. It seems to me a hideous mockery if we spend millions of dollars on science in order to make it possible for people to live longer, and cannot meet the challenge properly by providing for [DOT]them decently.
I support a contributory system, but I have no delusion about it at all. I know its coverage is incomplete. I know that under the contributory system in Britain twenty per cent of the people are not covered, while in the United States forty per cent are not covered; and I know that the pension is very small. I know that in New Zealand after ten years of payment into the contributory pension fund a person is able to draw only $9 a month, while in the United States after fifteen years of payment a person draws only $26 a month. They need supplementary assistance, and they apply the means test. So if any of us are telling the people that if we add a contributory system to the system we have at the present time, with a means test, this will be the answer to our problem, we are

wrong in telling them that, because that will not solve any problem for us at the present time. It may solve a problem thirty years from now, but not today; it is confusing and misleading, and if we are giving that impression we ought to stop doing so.
My feeling is that there is only one solution. I believe we must have a universal pension plan under which everyone is covered, farmer, self-employed, domestic; everyone must be covered, and there must be a guaranteed minimum at a fixed age. We should pay for it in the way we pay for other things, by a social security tax which ought to be imposed to the extent we can afford. Here is an opportunity for us to do some original thinking on this problem comparable to the thinking we did in connection with the family allowance. Our family allowance legislation was copied; we were praised for it everywhere. So far in connection with this problem we have been groping, and I think it is time we started thinking it through.
When we speak of a contributory system, that will look after the future of those who are working today; but what about the present? Are we doing for those aged people what we expect will be done for us? Are we not penalizing the older workers because we procrastinated and failed to introduce a contributory system many years ago? Why, the labour unions of this country have been pleading for a system of that kind for as long as I can remember. Now we have on the scene the new industrial pensions. They are no longer academic; they are really here. The unions are concentrating upon retirement pensions and disability and sickness benefits; and they have made progress in the United States in textiles, in automobiles, in rubber and in the mining industry.

Yes; I thought the mining industry covered coal. I said we have some 464 plans in Canada covering textiles, pulp, mining and some other industries. At the present time we have before us the Ford plan which provides $55 a month, subject to a means test; but the unions are prepared to fight to a finish for their demand that the pensions be free of a means test. It may surprise hon. members to learn that management regards their request as very reasonable in principle, and supports it. I could read some statements by management which might surprise hon. members. Here we have the United States chamber of commerce appearing before a committee in Washington requesting that the minimum benefits paid to a family should be increased from $85 to $120. That is something new; but it shows how aware they have become of these problems.

Old Age Security
The tendency has been for the labour contract in the Canadian branches to conform with that of the parent plant in the United States if the situation is the same in both countries. The joker is that the situation is not the same in both countries. Here lies a potential cause of great industrial strife, and that is one reason labour and industry are pressing so hard for a solution of this pension problem. In the United States they have a pension base. As I have indicated already, after contributing for fifteen years there is a pension base of $26, which in some instances may be somewhat increased. In the United States the worker has an opportunity to build on that pension. He may do so as a result of collective industrial agreements or from his personal savings. We have no such base in Canada, because we have the means test, which is the big stumbling block. I think the time has come when we in Canada should have a universal pension with a minimum guaranteed as a floor under poverty.
The hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) asked some questions, and I am going to ask this question. Here we have two men working in the same plant, receiving the same wages, having been employed for the same number of years. One scrimps and denies himself to buy an annuity which will pay him $40 a month at the age of seventy, and finally he gets that annuity. The other man saves nothing, but at the age of seventy he draws $40 a month in old age pension, and if he is lucky enough to live in British Columbia he gets $50. Should we not try to correct a situation like that? You may say there is something the matter with the man but I believe there is something the matter with a system which permits that sort of thing.
Let us look at some of the larger plants. I will agree that Ford, Chrysler, General Motors and Goodyear can pay pensions; but can the smaller plants employing fifteen, twenty, thirty or forty men pay pensions, and if they do, will their pensions be the same? In order to have harmony in this country are we not obligated to see that we have a plan upon which people can build? Have we not a responsibility, particularly where we grant tax exemptions, to see that pensions are paid every month and every year for life? The government should have something to say about those pension plans when they give tax exemptions. I can think of no greater catastrophe that might befall this country than if some of the pension plans could not pay off when they ought to. So the government must safeguard, it must certify, in the same way that it handles insurance companies at the present time. I have said that my own feeling in the matter was that
[Mr. Croll.l
we ought to have a universal pension, in the same way as we have family allowances. It has an advantage. You may think of some disadvantages. I know what crops up in your minds: can we afford it? I shall deal with that problem in a moment or two. A universal pension gives Canadians uniformity of treatment, and it averts formidable administrative problems.
This thought occurs to me. I know quite well that the industrial workers will get their pension, even if they have to hammer it out on the picket line. Everyone knows that. What will happen under those circumstances if the farmer, who also makes a contribution to the economy of the country, finds himself paying for the industrial worker's pension while, at the same time, not having one for himself? Are we not asking for trouble? I think the time has come when we must provide a basis that will permit all individuals, whether they are farmers or labourers, to build upon that base with their savings. The industrial worker could, at the same time, build upon it through his collective agreements. You must not forget that what goes to the industrial worker by way of a pension is deferred wages, and it must be non-contributory. Then the provinces may supplement the pension.
I welcome this committee, because I feel the country is looking for guidance, leadership and action. The usual objection to a universal pension is that it will cost money. Of course it will cost money. Are we not paying too big a price in this country in fear and insecurity? Must we not look at this as a great human problem, rather than as a financial problem? I feel certain that we can afford the $200 million or $250 million we were talking about. In addition to that, it seems to me that if I were living outside the province of Ontario, I should look at the redistribution of wealth such a scheme brings about. There is a levelling process going on, as there is with family allowances, and it is a levelling up.
I come from the province of Ontario, and we pay 45 -5 per cent of the taxes in Canada. We collect in family allowances 29 per cent of the tax. Some 16 per cent, therefore, is levelled out through the other parts of Canada. The same thing would be true with respect to universal pensions. In Ontario we would only be receiving 24 per cent of any pensions that were paid, so there would be 21 per cent more of that money that would be distributed to the less fortunate parts of Canada. I have always believed that if I raised the standard of living of a man in Saskatoon I improved the job possibilities of a man in Spadina.
I feel that the true measure of our strength as a nation is not our military establishments

alone, but the vigour, health and spirit of the people themselves. That is what makes up the living tissue of Canadian democracy, and that is our greatest all-round defence, come what may. I realize that I have not been very specific about a universal pension. I believe, however, that if we endorse the principle, we will not have any difficulty in agreeing on the details. I agree with the statement by the member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), and what was repeated by the member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), that the money to be paid must come from the national product. The man who works must pay for the benefits going to the man who cannot work. Employers will charge their contribution to the cost of doing business; therefore in some instances consumers may have to pay higher prices- although from the appearance of profit sheets which are published now and then in our newspapers, I would not know why. In short, the man who has earned a loaf of bread must share a slice or two with his needy neighbour.
In all the history I have read, I have never read about a state that went broke by reason of underwriting a social minimum for its citizens. I have, however, read of states that disappeared because they did not do it. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that this motion, which gives us an opportunity to hold an open forum on pensions, which gives us the opportunity of having men, women and organizations come before us to present their views, will have an educational value in this country. People will more readily understand what our problem is, and perhaps will help us to reach a solution.
Last session we passed what I considered a very important amendment to the housing act. It is beginning to bear fruit for the people of Canada in the form of more and better houses. I believe that this parliament can write its name indelibly in the history of our country by bringing in a universal security measure which will make those homes secure for the people. I intend to support the motion.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE TO STUDY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the first occasion on which I have had the pleasure of immediately following the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll). I should like to congratulate him on a very fine speech which this house has enjoyed during the last few minutes. I agree with him, Mr. Speaker, in welcoming the motion to set up the proposed committee. The wording of the motion outlines the government's intention to hold a full examination of our old age pension system. The government is turning to the proper instrument of parliament in order to carry out that examination under our parliamentary system.
The subject of old age pensions is one which is being discussed a great deal these days,
Old Age Security
both in this house and throughout the country. It is quite apparent, I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the extent of the problems involved in expanding our old age pensions, as well as other social security measures, is not fully understood by some individuals in this house, or by many individuals throughout the country. Since the opening of this session we have heard members calling for increased pensions, the removal of the means test, and other changes in our present system. From this it would seem to be clear that we should at least take a searching look at the question of old age security in this country, and come to some conclusions upon it.
For example, the Prime Minister, in speaking at Vancouver on April 14, 1949, said:
We are certainly not satisfied with our old age pension legislation, even though the scale of pensions is 50 per cent higher in dollars than it was before the war.
We have had old age pensions in this country, Mr. Speaker, for 23 years. It is still an interim program which has been improved and extended on five occasions in that 23 years. I agree to some extent with the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) who said this afternoon that in the past we had dealt with old age pensions in a not too well organized manner. The changes that have been made have been forward steps and as far as they went they have been productive of good to the social well-being of the people of this country. The government is proposing today to the hon. member for Eglinton and all hon. members of this house that we use a committee of parliament in order to look at the whole question, to see how we have progressed in the past, to see how we should move in the future in order that extensions of this program will not be open to criticism of having been adopted without full consideration of all the circumstances. For that reason I submit that much of the opposition expressed this afternoon by the hon. member to the setting up of a committee was illogical and not well taken.
There are four main points around which the discussion of the extension of our old age security program has revolved. These are:
1.	The abolition of the means test.
2.	The reduction of the age at which men and women shall become entitled to old age assistance.
3.	The payment of pensions on a higher scale than at present.
4.	The introduction of a contributory system of old age pensions.
In order to illustrate some of the important and complex problems which have to be considered in dealing with this question, I should like to discuss briefly each of the four points which I have mentioned and which have been referred to by previous speakers in this

Old Age Security
debate to some extent or other. At the present time we are paying old age pensions on a means-test basis to persons over seventy years of age. There are approximately 625,000 people over the age of seventy years, and some 42 or 43 per cent or approximately 265,000 are receiving 'old age pensions of $40 per month, plus certain additions in various provinces, on a means-test basis. The pensions now being paid involve an expenditure of over $100 million on federal account, something over $33 million on provincial account, or a total of $133 million.
Suppose we consider putting into practice what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) referred to this afternoon as the first step in improving and extending our old age security program, that is, the abolition of the means test. By doing that one thing alone we would increase the annual cost of a $40 pension to all persons over seventy years of age to $300 million a year, or an additional $200 million.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre pointed out that the speakers who had preceded him had not suggested any concrete step that should be taken with respect to abolishing the means test or anything else. He said that he was satisfied that the first step we should take was to abolish the means test. However, he did not go any further and explain just where he thought the additional $200 million that would be required to take that step was to come from. I am not saying that we will not have to find that money, but the point I want to make is that if the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre or any other hon. member is going to come to grips with this problem he will have to say, not whether we should do thus and so but that we should do thus and so and the money will come from such and such a source.
The purpose of this committee is to study what we should do and how we are to provide the funds wherewith to do it. The hon. member cannot point the finger of scorn at any hon. member in this house for not making a concrete suggestion when he himself makes only half a concrete suggestion in saying, "Abolish the means test", but omitting to say anything about where the money is to come from. That is one consideration we have to keep in mind when we say, abolish the means test.
The second suggestion is the reduction of the age of eligibility for pension. Suppose that in addition to abolishing the means test we considered that the time has come when the age of eligibility should be reduced. One suggestion that has been made outside the house is that the age of eligibility for women should

be reduced to sixty-five years while the age of eligibility for men should be kept at seventy years, with a $40 pension for all. To pay a $40 pension to all women who had reached the age of sixty-five years and to men who had reached the age of seventy years would cost $390,624,000 this year. If we were to lower the age of eligibility for both men and women to sixty-five years, the cost this year would be $491 million, or almost $500 million.
I point out these figures merely to show the problem that has to be met, not to say what should or should not be done or what we can afford or what we cannot afford. I simply point out that in advocating these changes we must come to grips with the problem of how they are to be paid for. Suppose it is decided that a pension of $40 is not sufficient. Many in this house have argued strenuously that this is an absolute minimum pension that has to be added to; that it cannot be left at that level. Suppose we decide that a minimum pension of $50 would meet the present requirements. For a pension of $50 at age sixty-five the bill this year would be $614 million, and by 1971 the pension bill on that basis would be $960 million, almost $1 billion. That shows the extent of the problem that we have to meet.
I have dealt with three of the points that I mentioned earlier. The last one, the introduction of a contributory system, has been dealt with more fully by some of the speakers who preceded me in this debate. However, I should like to point out that any system is a contributory system. The money comes from the production of the country and goes into the fund, either the general fund of government through taxation, or into a special fund from special taxes which are called contributions. Simply by saying that it is a contributory system does not change one iota the expense involved. It simply is a suggestion of methods of raising the money that is required.
The committee is being empowered to look into and to examine all these important complex questions. I say to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), with respect, that in my view the wording of the resolution is as wide as could possibly be expected within the limits of the English language; that the power that he wishes the committee to have, as expressed by his amendment, is there in the wording that has been used, and that we would simply, by adopting his amendment, be saying the same thing twice.

speechtext:
It would do you a lot of good, though. I do not think it is necessary to adopt the amendment.
In addition to these questions that I have outlined there are other important problems that the committee will have to face. Because of the legislative authority of the provinces on property and civil rights there is involved in this question a constitutional problem which must be solved by agreement with the provinces. In passing I might point out, Mr. Speaker, that that is not always an easy problem to solve. The agreement with all the provinces to bring into effect the system that we now have took nine years from the time of the passage of this act in 1927. It was 1936 before the last two provinces came in and joined in that scheme. That is another problem that the committee is going to have to consider.
The committee is going to have to consider the opinions of many people who do not all agree. For instance, there is general agreement that something should be done about the means test. I agree with what the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) had to say in that respect; but there are many people who have expressed the opinion to me. that the first thing to do is to make sure that we are providing for all the needy cases before we provide public funds to pay old age pensions to people who clearly do not need them, and that would be one result of removing the means test.
The hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) made a plea which has been expressed in this house before, namely, that attention be paid to the needs of the incurables. Many people in this country think that some action should be taken about that before we pay pensions on a no means test basis. Many people feel that other aspects of our social security program need attention before some of the problems arising out of old age pensions.
I should like to add something to what the hon, member for Spadina has said about industrial pensions and the view being taken by many people in industry in this country today about the means test. Many hon. members seem to think that, when they rise in their places and say, "we must do away with the means test", they are saying something that is unique and does not meet with general agreement. I think that today in this country it does meet with general agreement. Just over two months ago I heard the president of one of the greatest corporations in this country tell a meeting of a board of trade that he felt the means test was working a hardship on the employees of his company who had a company-financed retirement fund and retirement scheme, and that some conoid Age Security
sideration should be given to adjusting the means test to remove any unfairness to men in that category.
In conclusion, I should simply like to say that all hon. members who think that they have access to all the information which may have a bearing on this subject, or even those who think that all the information that is necessary to make a wise decision on this question is in the possession of some hon. members-all hon. members who think that they have the answers to these questions, and all hon. members who are satisfied that they can stand up and say to the people of this country, "I have a solution to this whole problem which is bound to be the right one, and which takes into consideration everything that should be considered"-should vote against this resolution and the committee because the committee is not necessary. To all those hon. members who, like myself and the hon. member for Spadina, feel that there is a great deal of information on this question that we have not been able to obtain, and have not been able to comprehend-who feel that they have not all the answers to these questions and that in order to carry out our responsibilities to the people of Canada we should see that all these questions are gone into with the greatest care and as fully as the powers of this parliament will permit-I say they agree with the hon. member for Spadina and myself and should vote for this motion and be glad to see this committee set up.

No one had sent word to Mr. Speaker that he was to speak before me. My name followed that of the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey). However, I do not want to take the place of the hon. member for Royal, and if he wishes to proceed I shall be happy to take my seat.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE TO STUDY
speechtext:
Thank you, sir.
Mr. Speaker, this resolution contains in the first paragraph a summary of the whole social question. I congratulate the industrious and diligent Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) on having sponsored it today. It is timely for members of parliament to meet together and to discuss all these questions without partisan spirit, in an effort to come to the most satisfactory conclusions for all.

Old Age Security
As the junior member for Halifax has pointed out, we shall consider the whole matter objectively for the good of those who are to benefit from any enactment by parliament. At this stage I should like to congratulate all those who have spoken on this most important matter. May I remind the house that some personal friends of mine, the hon. member for Terrebonne (Mr. Bertrand), the hon. member for Compton-Frontenac (Mr. Blanchette) and the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Picard), have taken a particular interest in the matter.
I agree that hon. members In the Progressive Conservative party, the C.C.F. group and the Social Credit group, and even my independent friend from Chicoutimi (Mr. Gagnon), are also interested in the matter. No one should contend that he is more interested in it than anybody else, because we are all interested and are trying to do our best for the people of Canada, especially those who suffer from disability and who are in an unfortunate condition that can be remedied at least partially.
Any member of parliament meets a large number of people. I am not boasting, but I state as a fact that when I am at home I see between fifty and sixty callers a day at my office. I do not practise law; my parliamentary duties do not leave me the leisure to practise my profession as I did before. I take a case occasionally, but I cannot follow the practice regularly.
My office is almost a drawing room or a reception room for those who come to see me and tell me about their troubles. And, sir, you will realize that when a poor man comes to you to disclose to you his intimate feelings and to tell you troubles he would confess to no one except a friend, you feel honoured by that confidence. This happens very often. Constituents will go to their member of parliament for the redress of their wrongs and to tell him their troubles.
This is the only way one can become informed as to the effect of legislation passed by parliament. People come to us in all confidence and speak openly, asking for something. That is legitimate. I do not complain about it; and so long as we keep our mandate to represent the people of Canada we have to do it. It is part of our job; I am not complaining, and the day I feel like complaining I shall resign with the feeling that I am no longer fit to be a member of parliament.
From the stories told to us of the intimate events of the lives of our constituents we can form a composite picture. Each member of parliament who listens to his constituents has in mind that same composite picture of the happiness and misery of certain sections of the Canadian people. Those with whom
I sympathize most are the ones whom, in French, we describe as "les pauvres en habit noir", the poor who are just as well dressed as they can afford to be. They try to make the best of it. They are too proud to beg but, for the sake of appearances, they show up as best they can. No one should be insensible to the approach of these people who are so proud, but who will come to someone to tell them their handicaps and their disabilities. No one should fail to pay attention to what is said in order some day to be in a position to help them.

One moment more. When I say this I feel sure I am expressing the feelings of my colleagues in the House of Commons who have been in similar positions- and I am sure all have been.
Therefore I consider this problem placed before us by the minister as one of the most important to be discussed by parliament. Light comes from discussion. While this is not the only important subject for our consideration, certainly it is important, and we must not take for granted that every request will be acceded to.
When the old age pension was granted with only one condition attached, namely that of age, I stated sincerely that a mistake had been made. I have repeated that to my constituents, and have received a good response to what I have said. In my view, age should not be the factor in granting a pension; rather, it should be need. There are men and women who have not reached the age of seventy but who are deserving of pensions. Proof of this is that pensions for the blind are given to younger people; parliament has agreed to that, the only objection being that the age was not low enough.
Before concluding I shall make only one further observation, following which I shall adjourn the debate. Pensions will be paid from taxes; but pensions to the disabled will be paid from taxes paid by people who are not so unfortunate and who, although disabled, are in a position to earn their living. The higher the pensions will be, the lees will the taxpayers be in a position to pay for them.
I move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.
